overview: The atlas begins this record in 1920, during Portuguese colonial rule. Guinea-Bissau proclaimed independence on 24 September 1973; Portugal formally recognized it the following year. The card follows that transition and the continuing country, whose mainland communities and Bijagós islands have distinct languages, farming knowledge and artistic traditions.

periods.title: Portuguese Guinea and liberation
periods.summary: The imported starting date belongs to the colonial period.

periods.title: Proclamation and recognition
periods.summary: Proclamation in September 1973 preceded Portuguese recognition in September 1974.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: Independence continued despite later political conflict.

items.text: Two dates matter in the independence story. The People’s National Assembly proclaimed the state on 24 September 1973. Portugal’s president signed recognition on 10 September 1974, after negotiations. Calling 1920 the country’s independence year would confuse an atlas snapshot with the end of colonial government.

Independence did not end political conflict. The US diplomatic history records the suspension of its Bissau embassy operations on 14 June 1998 because of civil war. That was a disruption to government and ordinary lives within the republic, rather than the disappearance of Guinea-Bissau as a country.

Before becoming a liberation leader, Amílcar Cabral worked as an agricultural scientist. From November 1953 to April 1954, his survey team included fellow agronomist Maria Helena Rodrigues, his wife. They investigated 2,248 family holdings in 356 villages, using sampling rather than pretending they could inspect every farm.

Cabral’s published graph compared cultivated, burned and fallow land. It distinguished rice-growing and peanut-growing systems and questioned colonial enthusiasm for cash crops. A chart about soil could carry a political argument: farmers’ knowledge and the future of their land belonged at the centre of discussions about development.

A December 1964 PAIGC circular announced “Nosso Primeiro Livro de Leitura,” meaning “Our First Reading Book.” The document survives in the Amílcar Cabral archive. Publishing a beginner’s reader during the liberation struggle shows education as practical organizing work: a political movement also needed children and adults who could read.

Here is a short Kriyol sentence recorded by linguists: “N tene kaneta.” It means “I have a pen.” The 2013 APiCS language survey prints this as example 9 in its explanation of verbs. It is an attested modern teaching example, written in the Latin alphabet.

Kriyol connects speakers of different home languages in markets, public services and everyday conversation. The same linguistic survey describes experiments using it in bilingual education. Portuguese has a different formal role, while local African languages remain important: a child’s home, street and classroom need not sound exactly alike.

The Bijagós coastal and marine ecosystems entered the World Heritage List in 2025. Mangroves, mudflats and shallow channels shelter fish, turtles and migrating birds. Poilão is especially important for green-turtle nesting. The protected property covers selected high-value ecosystems, rather than turning every island into one undifferentiated nature reserve.

UNESCO credits local communities’ customary management alongside government conservation work. Marine protected areas created in 2000 and 2005 include the Urok Islands community area. Protecting the archipelago therefore involves people deciding how places and resources are used, as well as scientists counting animals.

sections.title: Water and the work of healthier homes

items.text: In Quinara, sanitation meetings often took place under a mango tree. UNICEF’s 2019 account describes facilitators helping residents map where waste went and how flies, rainwater and hands could carry it home. The discussion was memorable because it connected an uncomfortable subject to the places families knew.

Families then built toilets with local materials. Quinara received open-defecation-free recognition in 2018, and follow-up visits checked continued use and hygiene practices. Soap and handwashing were part of the achievement. The useful invention here was also organizational: neighbours worked together to keep their surroundings cleaner.

A smartphone could help find a broken pump. UNICEF reports that mWATER mapping, begun in 2016 and continued in 2018, visited nearly 5,250 water points. Recording whether a pump actually worked made the map useful for repairs; a dot labelled “water” is not much help when the handle produces nothing.

ending.text: Portuguese colonial rule ended through the 1973 proclamation and 1974 recognition. Guinea-Bissau continues as a republic; later conflict and changes of government did not end the country or its communities.
